source.title: Exploring how OthelloGPT computes its world model

page_placements.theme: Rule-like neurons in small game- or task-trained models (OthelloGPT, Sudoku, DRL agents, numeric succession)

record.tranche_reason: The post reports a neuron-rule classification and ablation test that the author says provides mild evidence against individual neurons performing interpretable rules, but it does not test any listed version's specific audit share or explanation-scoring procedure.
record.gate_note: The post also reports attention-circuit and legal-move results, which do not measure neuron-job shares or the explanation tests specified in the versions. Its citation to the earlier OthelloGPT post is not a result from this study.
record.test_reason: The study works on OthelloGPT, a small transformer trained on Othello move sequences. It classifies MLP neurons against hand-defined tile-flipping rules and tests whether those neurons alone reproduce flip decisions under mean ablation. None of the listed versions is measured: there is no share of neurons with one, two or unknown jobs, no language model at scale, no vision neuron, no neuron-based attribution graph, and no scoring of explanations by predicting activations. The ablation tests whether the chosen neurons are causally sufficient, which is a different construct from V6's question of where a neuron fires. The result therefore goes under fits_no_version rather than as a test. I changed the reader's T5 to T6 because the argument is aimed at the 'bag of heuristics' account of OthelloGPT, not at any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The author says the failed ablation gives mild evidence against individual OthelloGPT neurons performing interpretable rules. The author also says only a very specific rule set was tested, the classification threshold could have been stricter, and a code bug is possible because only one example was checked thoroughly.
record.recipe_differences: The post uses rule-based neuron classification and ablation in OthelloGPT, rather than pole-level job audits or held-out explanation scoring.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports that the previous-color circuit's accuracy varied by layer, sequence position, and board location; the flipping-circuit accuracy is presented across layers and separately for board center and rim.

fits_no_version.finding: In OthelloGPT, neurons that looked monosemantic by weight projection were classified against tile-flipping rules. Keeping only those rule neurons and mean-ablating the rest did not beat mean-ablating all neurons when predicting flips, except in later layers where many neurons stayed unablated.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons that look rule-like by weight projection and activation difference may not be causally sufficient to carry out the inferred rule (OthelloGPT, flipping rules).

record.problems: The rule set was specific; the author says only one example was thoroughly checked and notes a possible code bug. The post does not report exact numerical values for the neuron-count histogram or the ablation accuracy comparison in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The post's previous-color circuit measurements concern attention layers rather than the neuron-job claim. The legal-move ablation result concerns a different outcome. Neither was included as a row.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or of job shares.
No job-share estimates for any language model, dense or mixture-of-experts, or at any scale; OthelloGPT is a board-game toy model.
No vision neurons and no test of recursive generalization.
No comparison of architecture, regularization or tools, and no interpretable-share estimate.
No attribution graphs built from the model's own neurons.
No test of whether explanations from activating examples predict where a neuron fires on held-out data.

record.verdict_notes: This is a bachelor's-thesis write-up posted on LessWrong; no peer review is stated. The attention-layer 'previous color circuit' results (overall accuracy 0.818) and the legal-move ablation result were rightly left out as rows, since neither bears on neuron-job claims. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate shares with one, two, or unknown jobs.
It does not estimate comparable shares across models, architectures, or scales.
It does not examine InceptionV1's cat-and-car neuron or recursive generalization.
It does not compare architecture, regularization, or tools, or estimate interpretability rates for vision models.
It does not test attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons.
It does not test explanations against held-out activation examples to measure whether they predict where a neuron fires.
It does not score explanations by simulating neuron activations on new text.

relation.reason: The post discusses neuron interpretability in OthelloGPT (against the bag-of-heuristics view) without testing any listed version.

tranche.reason: The post tests a hand-defined tile-flipping rule hypothesis for OthelloGPT neurons. It does not measure any version's audit share, scoring or attribution-graph claim. Its failed ablation is a different construct, though the pack's earlier reader call was T5.

source_check.notes: All three rows are figure-only with no exact values, and none links to a version. R1 is the neuron-to-rule selection step for the ablation, not a result. Neurons are assigned to rules by activation difference above 0.17, not by weight projection. The author flags a possible code bug, since only one example was checked thoroughly.

statements.correction: Rules: tile t marked Yours, flip direction F, n Mine tiles to flip. A neuron follows a rule if its mean activation difference over 10,000 games is above 0.17. For each move, all neurons except those of the active rules were mean-ablated. Measure: accuracy of the flipped-probe readout against the unablated run, on tiles whose flipped status changes at that layer. Result: no better than the baseline of mean-ablating all neurons, except in later layers, where many neurons were not ablated. The author calls this mild evidence against neurons performing interpretable rules. Caveats from the author: only a specific rule set was tested, the threshold was lenient, and a code bug is possible.
statements.problem: Neurons were not selected by weight projection. They were assigned to hand-defined flip rules by mean activation difference above 0.17 over 10,000 games. Weight projections were only how the author first noticed flipping neurons, e.g. L1N1411. Only neurons for the rules active on that move were kept. The statement leaves out that the later-layer exception is confounded, since many neurons go unablated there.
